items.prompt: What are the three types of muscle tissue found in vertebrates?

options.label: Striated, smooth, and cardiac
options.feedback: Striated is a description, not a type; the actual types are skeletal, cardiac, and smooth.

options.label: Skeletal, cardiac, and smooth
options.feedback: Correct. These are the three muscle tissues in vertebrates, each with distinct locations and control.

options.label: Voluntary, involuntary, and reflex
options.feedback: Those describe how muscles are controlled, not the tissue types themselves.

options.label: Red, white, and mixed
options.feedback: These refer to muscle fiber colors, not the three tissue types.

items.ok_line: Skeletal, cardiac, and smooth are the three.
items.exp_text: Vertebrates have skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle tissue. Skeletal and cardiac are striated, while smooth is not. Each plays a different role in the body.

items.prompt: Which two muscle types contract involuntarily, without conscious effort?

options.label: Skeletal and cardiac
options.feedback: Skeletal muscle is voluntary; only cardiac contracts without your conscious control.

options.label: Smooth and skeletal
options.feedback: Skeletal is voluntary, so this pair is wrong.

options.label: Cardiac and smooth
options.feedback: Correct. Both work automatically, controlled by the autonomic nervous system or hormones.

options.label: Only skeletal
options.feedback: Skeletal is actually voluntary, so this is incorrect.

items.ok_line: Cardiac and smooth work on their own.
items.exp_text: Cardiac and smooth muscle contract without conscious thought. Skeletal muscle, in contrast, is voluntary and needs your decision to move.

items.prompt: What gives skeletal muscle its striped appearance?

options.label: Sarcomeres arranged in regular bundles
options.feedback: Correct. The regular parallel arrangement of myofibrils and their sarcomeres creates the striations.

options.label: The presence of many blood vessels
options.feedback: Blood vessels supply oxygen but do not cause the stripes.

options.label: The layer of fat around the muscle
options.feedback: Fat is separate tissue, not part of the muscle's internal structure.

options.label: The tendons at both ends
options.feedback: Tendons anchor muscle to bone, but they do not make the muscle look striped.

items.ok_line: Sarcomeres line up to make stripes.
items.ko_line: Stripes come from inside the fibers.
items.exp_text: Skeletal muscle fibers contain many myofibrils, and within them are sarcomeres arranged in regular parallel bundles. This repeating pattern gives the tissue its striped, or striated, look.

items.prompt: Where is cardiac muscle tissue found?

options.label: In the walls of the stomach and intestines
options.feedback: Those contain smooth muscle, not cardiac muscle.

options.label: In the walls of blood vessels
options.feedback: Blood vessels have smooth muscle, called vascular smooth muscle.

options.label: Attached to the bones of the skeleton
options.feedback: That is skeletal muscle, not cardiac muscle.

options.label: Only in the walls of the heart
options.feedback: Correct. Cardiac muscle forms the myocardium, the heart's muscular wall.

items.ok_line: Cardiac muscle is only in the heart.
items.ko_line: Those other places use smooth muscle.
items.exp_text: Cardiac muscle is found exclusively in the heart's walls, as the myocardium. It is striated but involuntary, unlike skeletal muscle.

items.prompt: Which muscle type is non-striated and involuntary?

options.label: Skeletal muscle
options.feedback: Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary, so it does not fit.

options.label: Smooth muscle
options.feedback: Correct. Smooth muscle has no stripes and works automatically.

options.label: Cardiac muscle
options.feedback: Cardiac is involuntary but it is striated, not non-striated.

options.label: Type II muscle
options.feedback: Type II refers to fast-twitch skeletal fibers, which are still striated and voluntary.

items.ok_line: Smooth is both non-striated and involuntary.
items.ko_line: Skeletal and cardiac don't match both.
items.exp_text: Smooth muscle is found in organ walls like the stomach and blood vessels, and it contracts without conscious control. It lacks the sarcomere pattern that gives other muscles stripes.

items.prompt: What are the two main types of skeletal muscle fibers?

options.label: Red and white
options.feedback: Those are descriptive colors, but the official classification is Type I and Type II.

options.label: Slow and fast only
options.feedback: Slow and fast are the common names, but the formal types are Type I and Type II.

options.label: Type I (slow-twitch) and Type II (fast-twitch)
options.feedback: Correct. Skeletal muscle fibers are broadly split into these two categories.

options.label: Cardiac and smooth
options.feedback: Those are different muscle tissues, not fiber types within skeletal muscle.

items.ok_line: Type I and Type II are the two.
items.ko_line: The classification is Type I and Type II.
items.exp_text: Skeletal muscle is broadly divided into Type I slow-twitch fibers and Type II fast-twitch fibers. These differ in speed, endurance, and how they get energy.

items.prompt: What is the main characteristic of Type I (slow-twitch) muscle fibers?

options.label: They are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, giving them a red color
options.feedback: Correct. This allows them to carry oxygen and sustain aerobic activity.

options.label: They contract very quickly and tire fast
options.feedback: That describes fast-twitch Type II fibers, not Type I.

options.label: They are white and low in myoglobin
options.feedback: White, low-myoglobin fibers are Type IIb, not Type I.

options.label: They are found only in the heart
options.feedback: Type I fibers are skeletal muscle, not cardiac muscle.

items.ok_line: Type I is red, oxygen-rich, and enduring.
items.exp_text: Type I fibers are dense with capillaries, mitochondria, and myoglobin, which makes them red. They can carry more oxygen and sustain aerobic activity over time.

items.prompt: Which statement about cardiac muscle is true?

options.label: It is voluntary and striated
options.feedback: Cardiac muscle is involuntary, not voluntary, even though it is striated.

options.label: It is found in the walls of the stomach
options.feedback: The stomach wall contains smooth muscle, not cardiac muscle.

options.label: Its cells each have many nuclei
options.feedback: Cardiac muscle cells usually have one nucleus, though some have two to four.

options.label: It connects at branching, irregular angles
options.feedback: Correct. Unlike skeletal muscle's parallel bundles, cardiac muscle cells join at intercalated discs in irregular angles.

items.exp_text: Cardiac muscle cells are striated but connect at branching, irregular angles through intercalated discs. This arrangement differs from skeletal muscle's regular parallel bundles.

items.prompt: What is the approximate density of mammalian skeletal muscle tissue compared to fat?

options.label: It is the same as fat
options.feedback: No, muscle is denser than fat.

options.label: It is about 15% denser than fat
options.feedback: Correct. Muscle density is about 1.06 kg/liter, while fat is about 0.92 kg/liter.

options.label: It is about 15% less dense than fat
options.feedback: That is backwards; muscle is denser, not less dense.

options.label: It is twice as dense as fat
options.feedback: The difference is only about 15%, not double.

items.ko_line: Muscle packs more mass per volume.
items.exp_text: Skeletal muscle tissue has a density around 1.06 kg per liter, while adipose tissue is about 0.92 kg per liter. This makes muscle approximately 15% denser than fat.

items.prompt: From which embryonic structure do all muscles develop?

options.label: The sclerotome
options.feedback: The sclerotome forms vertebrae, not muscle.

options.label: The dermatome
options.feedback: The dermatome forms skin, not muscle.

options.label: The myotome
options.feedback: Correct. The myotome is the part of each somite that gives rise to muscle.

options.label: The hypomere only
options.feedback: The hypomere is a subdivision of the myotome, not the source of all muscles.

items.ko_line: Sclerotome and dermatome make other tissues.
items.exp_text: All muscles come from the myotome, one of three divisions of each somite in the embryo. The other divisions, sclerotome and dermatome, form vertebrae and skin, respectively.
